entries.title: Chicago marca el cierre del Dinastía Tour de Peso Pluma y Tito Double P
entries.summary: <p>El público de Chicago sin duda le dio a los primos Peso Pluma y Tito Double P el cierre final del Dinastía Tour que merecían, con tres noches sold out en el United Center llenas de agradecimiento este pasado fin de semana.</p><p>Con alrededor de 30 fechas, Chicago marcó el final de su gira por Estados Unidos, donde les llevaron a sus fans su álbum en conjunto, DINASTÍA, lanzado la Navidad pasada. En el corazón del proyecto destacan el legado, el orgullo mexicano y, sobre todo, la familia.</p><p>Con luces brillantes y una pantalla mostrándole al público lo que pasaba detrás del escenario, la canción “All of the Lights” del rapero Kanye West alocó a todos porque, si algo quedó claro, es que los primos conocen bien a su público mexicoamericano de Chicago.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-a60000" name="module-a60000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>“¿Quién quiere escuchar corridos esta noche?”, gritó Tito al micrófono mientras sonaba “Intro”, dando inicio a la noche.</p><p>Con referencias a la lucha libre en las visualizaciones y la promoción del tour, el diseño del escenario reflejó esa estética y le dio al público un acceso más cercano. El escenario contaba con escaleras en ambos lados que imitaban las esquinas de un ring de lucha libre, por donde Peso y Tito subían no solo para acercarse a los fans, sino también para reforzar la temática del show. Una segunda plataforma tambîen evocaba la forma de un cuadrilátero, terminando de transformar el escenario en una extensión del universo visual del Dinastía Tour.</p><p>Familias, jóvenes y seguidores fieles llenaron la arena, muchos vestidos de negro como parte de la identidad del tour. Cada letra fue cantada a todo volumen.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-0e0000" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Peso Pluma aprovechó para manifestar en voz alta diciendo que pronto agotaría las entradas del estadio del Soldier Field.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Proporcionada por Héctor Rodríguez</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>La noche comenzó con ambos compartiendo el escenario e interpretando temas como “7-3” y “billete” de su más reciente lanzamiento. Sus estilos encajan bien, con Peso adoptando un tono más áspero y pesado que recordaba a las características vocales de Tito.</p><p>Después, cada uno tomó su momento en solitario para interpretar algunos de sus mayores éxitos. Tito se apoderó del escenario con canciones como “EL LOKERON”, “NADIE” y “LINDA”, mientras que Peso puso a cantar al público con “QLONA” y “Lady Gaga”. Ambos se complementaban arriba del escenario, con rosarios iguales colgando de un lado a otro mientras corrían de punta a punta con una energía imparable, acompañados de bailarines e instrumentos en vivo.</p><p>La noche estaba perfectamente curada con invitados especiales como Julian Mercado, Armenta, e Ivan Cornejo, quien interpretó “RELOJ” con Peso, y un mini set de 21 Savage. Sí, 21 Savage salió al escenario e interpretó “redrum”, un momento de surrealismo mexicano perfecto que hacía mucho sentido.</p><p>Mucho de lo que caracteriza a Peso es su sonido distintivo, que mezcla los corridos tradicionales con flows y rimas que recuerdan al rap y al trap. Su apreciación e influencia de la cultura afroamericana se hace evidente al invitar a raperos como 21 Savage al escenario. En otras fechas del tour también subieron artistas como Boogie y Swae Lee.</p><p>Esa conexión se hizo aún más evidente en la forma en que el público respondió a la fusión de géneros, especialmente cuando las influencias del rap entraban en un setlist dominado por corridos, con temas como “AMG”. La colaboración de 2023 con Natanael Cano y <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/suenos-music-festival-chicago/2024/05/26/suenos-gabito-ballesteros-review-latino-music-festival-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>Gabito Ballesteros</u></a> sigue siendo un clásico que nos recuerda lo bien que Peso Pluma ha ayudado a difuminar las fronteras entre la música regional mexicana y los sonidos urbanos.</p><p>Como una de las ciudades con mayor población de la diáspora mexicana en Estados Unidos, esta parada se sintió profundamente simbólica. La primera presentación de Peso en Chicago no llegó <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/suenos-music-festival/2025/05/24/peso-pluma-returns-to-chicagos-suenos-festival-with-a-crowd-pleasing-set" target="_blank" >sino hasta 2025</a>, luego de que su set como cabeza del cartel en Sueños 2024 fuera <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2024/05/26/suenos-music-festival-peso-pluma-cancelled-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>cancelado</u></a> por condiciones climáticas, y otra aparición en el United Center también se viera cancelada por motivos de seguridad. </p><p>Sin embargo, desde entonces Chicago no le ha fallado: cada presentación en la ciudad ha sido un sold out.</p><p>Peso y Tito cerraron su tour con broche de oro. Sus fans fueron testigos de su vínculo en el escenario. No hubo nada más cercano o identificable que la amistad y el lazo entre ambos. Fue un asunto realmente familiar, una experiencia sumamente especial de presenciar que demostró que “la sangre no olvida su origen.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div Por un instante, pareció profundamente agradecido de poder compartir ese momento con su primo.</p><p>Pero a quien realmente le dio las gracias fue a sus fans de la clase trabajadora, recordándole a todos que “valemos”.</p><p>“Gracias por hacer esto por nosotros”, dijo Peso. “¡Chicago, gracias por esta tercera noche!”</p><p>Peso aprovechó para manifestar en voz alta diciendo que pronto agotaría las entradas del estadio Soldier Field. Aquí en Chicago lo esperamos.<br></p>

entries.title: White Sox reach .500 this late in season for first time since 2022
entries.summary: <p>It wasn’t THAT long ago that the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a>’ record was at .500. It just feels like it.</p><p>The Sox were 2-2 to end March of 2025.</p><p>Then they lost eight in a row and finished April at 7-23.</p><p>But never mind that now. After beating the Royals 6-5 on Wednesday, the Sox are 21-21. They haven’t been at .500 this late in a season since they finished the 2022 season at 81-81.</p><p>So surely, the roar that emanated from the Sox’ clubhouse and could be heard down the hall was in celebration of this achievement in the team’s yearslong rebuild. Surely, that came up amid the hooting and hollering.</p><p>“No,” shortstop Colson Montgomery said. “We know we’re in a really good spot. We’re not really looking at the standings because there’s still a lot of baseball left. It’s definitely a good achievement that we can look at right now and see that things are going in the right direction.”</p><p>Maybe manager Will Venable, who has been pushing all the right buttons with this team, has a greater appreciation for the accomplishment, having played in the big leagues for nine years, many more than most players on the Sox’ youthful roster have.</p><p>“Yeah, for sure,” Venable said in his typical low-key demeanor. “Your record matters, and we want to keep going from here. Obviously, want to keep playing good baseball and just continue to stack good days, and the record will take care of itself.”</p><p>Maybe that roar wasn’t from the Sox’ clubhouse. The team’s business-like approach to their play belies the age of its biggest contributors. And on Wednesday, that was Montgomery, who went 3-for-4 with two runs and an RBI, including what turned out to be a much-needed solo homer leading off the seventh inning.</p><p>That’s because, after being staked to a 6-3 lead in the ninth, closer Seranthony Dominguez allowed a two-out, two-run homer to Royals star Bobby Witt. Dominguez recovered to fan pinch hitter Jac Caglianone to end it.</p><p>“That was a huge run to be able to tack on there,” Venable said. “Gave our bullpen a little bit of breathing room, made the difference in the game.”</p><p>“I did my scouting on the guy,” Montgomery said of reliever John Schreiber. “I do scouting on relievers before the game just because of a scenario where I’m leading off the inning and I won’t have much time to look at the guy. I knew where I needed to look and was committed to the fastball, and he threw it there.”</p><p>The top of the seventh also loomed large. Reliever Jordan Hicks entered and promptly hit No. 8 batter Isaac Collins and allowed a pinch-hit single to Carter Jensen. That spelled trouble with the Royals’ 1-2-3 hitters coming up.</p><p>But Hicks stuck out Maikel Garcia and Bobby Witt swinging and caught Lane Thomas looking.</p><p>“Really impressive,” Venable said. “Hicksy is feeling really good right now, he’s in a really good spot. There’s been some times where we used him in different spots. For him to come in in that leverage spot there was amazing.”</p><p>What wasn’t amazing was starter Noah Schultz’s control — again. He walked five in 4⅓ innings, allowing three runs and two hits and striking out five. But the way the Sox are going lately, they were able to overcome it.</p><p>“You can just see everyone is starting to be their true self,” Montgomery said, “and I feel like when you’re your true self, that’s when you’re most confident. I think confidence is infectious. So I think that everyone’s just feeding off each other.”</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" id="list-4a0005" name="list-4a0005"></a><div class="PageList-header" > <div class="PageList-header-title-wrap" > <div class="PageList-header-title"> <a class="" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="{borderColor=#dfdfdf, pageNumber=1, inverseColors=false, footerBgColor=#000000, count=9892, bodyFont=font-3, showListNumbers=false, imagePositionHorizontal=null, rteBodyFont=font-3, headerBottomBorderColor=#111010, subTitle=null, items=[{category=[{items=[White Sox]}], type=Image, _styledTemplate=null, imageAlignment=null, categoryUrl=https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox, isFeatured=false, description=[{items=[“This is the most fun I’ve ever had playing baseball. entries.title: Will Venable: White Sox' enjoyment playing together making difference in results
entries.summary: <p>Outfielder Derek Hill played for five other major-league clubs before joining the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> in September. Though none of them finished above .500 in his time with them, his remark Tuesday about the Sox still was notable.</p><p>“This is the most fun I’ve ever had playing baseball. It’s incredible,” Hill said. “Every guy’s pulling from the same side. Whoever gets called up, traded over here, doesn’t matter.”</p><p>Hill said that after hitting a tiebreaking home run in the eighth inning and making a diving catch in the ninth, so maybe he was just caught up in the moment. Besides, many of the Sox’ players only know of losing with the organization, which has endured three consecutive 100-plus-loss seasons. How much fun could they possibly have?</p><p>But listening to others in the clubhouse, there might be something to Hill’s comments.</p><p>“I love my teammates here,” second baseman Chase Meidroth said. “We know what we’re playing for. It’s a lot more than for ourselves. We’re playing for each other. The energy is natural. It’s easy when you come to this locker room [because] you know you got this group of guys.”</p><p>Manager Will Venable thinks that’s one reason for the Sox’ revival, which had them within one game of .500 entering Wednesday for the third time this season. It also had them at 20 wins, which they didn’t reach last season until June 5 (20-43).</p><p>“I think that makes a very big difference,” Venable said of the players’ enjoyment playing with each other. “It helps these guys hold each other accountable, give each other energy every day and communicate well. We’re seeing it show up in everything that they do.</p><p>“It really started from day one, in everything that we do, it comes up that they believe in each other. Everything that we do in meetings on the field, we talk about games afterwards, I just get the sense that that connection is what’s making the difference.”</p><h3>AL Central parity</h3><p>The Sox entered Wednesday in second place, 1½ games behind the first-place Guardians, in a tightly packed American League Central. All five teams were separated by three games. Venable was asked whether he thought the division would stay so close.</p><p>“I have no idea. Teams go on runs,” he said. “You think about us and the fact that we’ve played five games against our divisional opponents, and it’s all against [the Royals]. So I really don’t have a good feel for the division outside just the records.</p><p>“We’ve got a long way to go. We’re excited no one has run off with it yet. We’ll just keep doing our thing.”</p><p>The Sox finally will face a division foe other than the Royals on May 25, when they open a seven-game homestand with the Twins and Tigers.</p><h3>Notes</h3><p>The game Wednesday was delayed in the fourth inning to treat a fan who had fallen into the Royals’ bullpen beyond the right-field wall. The fan was transported to a hospital for more treatment.</p><p>• Jen Pawol worked the plate, making her the first woman to call balls and strikes for an MLB game in Chicago.</p><p>• Catcher Kyle Teel went 1-for-4 with a run scored, a walk and a strikeout batting third as the designated hitter in his second injury rehab outing for Triple-A Charlotte. He homered in his first game Tuesday.</p><p>• Right-hander Prelander Berroa, who has been on the injured list since having Tommy John surgery in March 2025, was scheduled to begin a rehab assignment in the Arizona Complex League.</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" id="list-4a0005" name="list-4a0005"></a><div class="PageList-header" > <div class="PageList-header-title-wrap" > <div class="PageList-header-title"> <a class="" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="{borderColor=#dfdfdf, pageNumber=1, pullQuoteIcon=[{image=null, narrowImage=null, _template=/image/Image.hbs, alt=null}], pagination=[{body=[Next Page], href=?p=2, _template=/link/Link.hbs, contentId=null, pianoSectionSlug=null, target=null}], inverseColors=false, footerBgColor=#000000, count=9892, bodyFont=font-3, showListNumbers=false, imagePositionHorizontal=null, rteBodyFont=font-3, headerBottomBorderColor=#111010, items=[{media=[{alt=Royals White Sox Baseball, ampLink=null, _styledTemplate=null, _template=/image/Image.hbs, image={src=https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/73/e0/c812a5bd49e09d21ebacf86eb08e/ap26133083101791.jpg, width=6014, height=4010}, narrowImage={src=https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/73/e0/c812a5bd49e09d21ebacf86eb08e/ap26133083101791.jpg, width=6014, height=4010}}], type=Image, _styledTemplate=null, imageAlignment=null, categoryUrl=https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox, description=[{items=[“This is the most fun I’ve ever had playing baseball. entries.title: Joliet man charged in fatal shooting of Kenwood maintenance man last month
entries.summary: <p>A Joliet man has been arrested in the fatal shooting of an apartment building maintenance worker in Kenwood last month, according to Chicago police.</p><p>Gaddis Price Jr., 38, is accused of first-degree murder and felony possession of a controlled substance, police said.</p><p>On April 2, police responded about 5:35 p.m. to a person shot at the building in the 4500 block of South Drexel Boulevard. Officers found Alonzo Johnson, 42, in the lobby, shot in his left hand, right shoulder and chest, according to a police report.</p><p>Officers spoke to a witness who said a building resident had argued with Johnson, then returned to the lobby and shot the maintenance worker, the report said.</p><p>Johnson, who lived in the same block as the apartment building, was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center in serious condition. He died there at 8:06 p.m., according to the Cook County medical examiner’s office.</p><p>Price Jr. is expected in court Thursday.</p>

entries.title: Sky grind out ugly win against the Valkyries
entries.summary: <p>SAN FRANCISCO— You won't win many basketball games shooting 36% from the field. But the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> found a way Wednesday night against the Valkyries, holding Golden State to 29.3% from the field and 26.9% from three.</p><p>That latter was a gift. The Valkyries, who had been shooting over 40% on 35 three-point attempts per game, went cold. But the Sky's defense deserves credit too. Their perimeter pressure improved from the Portland opener, helped by the return of veteran guard Natasha Cloud.</p><p>The offense went the opposite direction. The trio of Skylar Diggins, Kamilla Cardoso and Rickea Jackson, which had hummed a few nights earlier, struggled to score. Cardoso and Jackson finished the first half a combined 2 for 14. The Sky were 0 for 10 from deep and 4 for 10 from the free-throw line in the period.</p><p>Ugly stuff.</p><p>But the Sky held their own defensively, limiting the Valkyries to 28 first-half points.</p><p>"When things weren't working for us offensively, we stayed in it defensively, which is good," guard Jacy Sheldon said.</p><p>The second half didn't get much prettier for either team, but coach Tyler Marsh thought the Sky's effort improved. And the team got timely contributions when they needed them.</p><p>One key stretch came with just under three minutes left in the fourth quarter, with the Sky up 60-58. The Valkyries forced Jackson into picking up her dribble and it looked like a broken play. But rookie Gabriela Jaquez made a timely back cut, and Jackson found her for an easy layup. Next trip down, Jackson hit a 3-pointer, her first of the game. Then on the defensive end, Sheldon came up with a steal.</p><p>And that's how you grind one out on the road.</p><p>"This is the type of team that we've wanted," Marsh said. "We shouldn't take it for granted that when we play defense like this, when we have the effort that we came out with in the second half, we can overcome those offensive struggles. We just kept sticking with it."</p><p>Sheldon thought the 69-63 win displayed the team's budding identity.</p><p>"We got a lot of dogs," Sheldon said. "We got a lot of competitors, ultra-competitors. As far as our identity goes, you got a team full of people who are going to give it their all every game."</p>

entries.title: Cubs' losing streak reaches four after rare misplay by second baseman Nico Hoerner
entries.summary: <p>ATLANTA — Cubs second baseman <b>Nico Hoerner’s</b> knack for improvising plays that defy belief has a flip side, though it rarely is seen.</p><p>The ‘‘Oh, wow’’ gives way to an ‘‘Oh, no.’’</p><p>With the Cubs and Braves tied at a run apiece in the eighth inning Wednesday, Hoerner saw <b>Michael Harris II</b> sprinting down the line on a slow roller and decided his only chance to get him out was to shovel the ball underhanded with his glove to first baseman <b>Michael Busch</b>.</p><p>To the Cubs’ horror, the ball went over Busch’s head. Harris reached safely, and a night of what manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> called ‘‘awesome . . . wonderful’’ pitching by <b>Shota Imanaga</b> was about to go into a death spiral.</p><p>Imanaga departed, then reliever <b>Phil Maton</b> hung a couple of curveballs — one that pinch hitter <b>Mike Yastrzemski</b> hit for a tiebreaking double and another that <b>Mauricio Dubon</b> launched into the left-field seats for a two-run home run.</p><p>Braves 4, Cubs 1.</p><p><b>Raisel Iglesias</b>, who has yet to be scored on this season, finished off the Cubs in the ninth for his eighth save, and the Braves became the first team in the majors to reach 30 victories.</p><p>The Cubs, meanwhile, have their first four-game losing streak of 2026. In two days, the Braves’ bullpen has held them to two singles in 10 scoreless innings. The Cubs have scored a total of three runs during their skid.</p><p>‘‘We made a lot of really nice plays tonight,’’ Counsell said on a night leather was flashed on both sides. ‘‘I’m sure Nico — it was a tough play, not an easy play — I’m sure he would tell you, ‘I could have made that play,’ but it was a tough play.’’</p><p>Counsell knows his second baseman.</p><p>‘‘I think I made it a harder play than it needed to be,’’ Hoerner said. ‘‘Just kind of misread the timing of it. Looking back on the play, there was definitely time to transfer to my hand.</p><p>“But you do rely on instincts all the time, and I trust that works most of the time. . . . But it definitely stings to have an error lead to the game-winning run.’’</p><p>The official scorer gave Harris a hit, and Imanaga was saddled with the loss on a night in which he set the Braves down in order in five of his seven-plus innings, didn’t walk a batter and allowed only five hits, including a home run to <b>Drake Baldwin</b> in the fourth.</p><p>The homer came on an out-of-the-zone slider that Baldwin had to reach for, but he nonetheless was strong enough to hit it 402 feet over the center-field wall.</p><p>Wonderful pitching? Imanaga wouldn’t go that far.</p><p>‘‘My outing, if I didn’t give up any runs, the Cubs would have had a chance to win,’’ he said. ‘‘So I think when I’m looking at it, you know, I should have kept it to zero.’’</p><h3>Giving Liam a look</h3><p>The Cubs are taking a flier on reliever <b>Liam Hendriks</b>, who won the hearts of White Sox fans in two seasons as their All-Star closer (2021-22), then tugged on their heartstrings with his very public — and successful — battle against Stage 4 non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma.</p><p>The Cubs signed Hendriks, 37, to a minor-league deal and initially plan to send him to their facility in Mesa, Arizona, with the expectation that he eventually will join Triple-A Iowa, Counsell said.</p><p>‘‘It’s essentially just depth right now and taking a shot at somebody who’s had a lot of success and see what happens,’’ Counsell said.</p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" entries.title: Fan hospitalized after falling into bullpen at Rate Field during White Sox, Royals game
entries.summary: <p>A fan was hospitalized after falling out of the stands and into a bullpen at Rate Field during the White Sox win against the Kansas City Royals Wednesday night.</p><p>The Chicago Sports Network, which was broadcasting the game Wednesday night, said on social media that a fan had fallen into the visiting team’s bullpen during the 4th inning and was taken to a nearby hospital. The incident caused a small delay during the fourth inning of the game.</p><p>“Hoping for a good recovery and health for the fan,” CHSN wrote on social media.</p><p>No information was available late Wednesday on the fan's condition. The hospital they were taken to also was not identified.</p><p>The Chicago Police Department and Chicago Fire Department didn’t immediately have details on the incident.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">There's an update regarding the delay in the 4th inning. A fan fell into the visiting team bullpen. That fan has now been transported to the hospital for treatment. <br><br>Hoping for a good recovery and health for the fan 🤞 <a href="https://t.co/dsHLFlUrL0">pic.twitter.com/dsHLFlUrL0</a></p>— White Sox on CHSN (@CHSN_WhiteSox) <a href="https://twitter.com/CHSN_WhiteSox/status/2054737326211846425?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">May 14, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.twitter.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/04/15/gerald-chaney-white-sox-game-national-anthem-performer-collapse" >White Sox national anthem performer Gerald Chaney back to singing after pre-game collapse</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: NFL schedule release: Bears will play Lions on Thanksgiving
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> are returning to Thanksgiving football on a much happier note.</p><p>They’ll travel to Ford Field in Detroit to play at noon on Nov. 26 this year, CBS announced Thursday morning. </p><p>The last time the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/05/13/bears-schedule-2026-not-part-international-slate-overseas-london-madrid-paris-rio-de-janeiro-melbourne-mexico-city-munich-nfl" target="_blank" >Bears</a> played the Lions at home in their traditional holiday spot, then-head coach Matt Eberflus botched his handling of the clock in a 2024 loss. He was fired upon returning to Chicago the next morning.</p><p>His replacement, Ben Johnson, fared much better in his first year, reaching the playoffs. However, he lost both games to his former employer, the Lions, last year. Johnson was the Lions' offensive coordinator before taking the Bears' job.</p><p>The Bears lost to the Lions in Week 2 and Week 18 last year. They've met each year since 1930, the longest uninterrupted matchup in league history. This year will mark the fifth time they've played at Ford Field on Thanksgiving in the past nine years — and the 20th time the two teams have met on the holiday.</p><p>The NFL will announce the full 2026 league schedule Thursday night. In addition to NFC North foes, the Bears will host the Buccaneers, Patriots, Saints, Eagles, Jaguars and Jets. They’ll play the Bills, Dolphins, Falcons, Panthers and Seahawks on the road.<br></p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: Man charged after shootout with cops in South Chicago
entries.summary: <p>A Chicago man who was shot by police during an exchange of gunfire was charged after the Monday shootout on the South Side. </p><p>Cordero Ramey, 26, was charged with attempted murder, unlawful use of a weapon and possession of a firearm as a felon, police said. </p><p>Ramey allegedly fired at officers and was shot and seriously wounded as they conducted an investigatory stop in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/12/man-seriously-wounded-in-shootout-with-police-in-south-chicago" target="_blank" >3100 block of East 83rd Street</a> around 10:30 p.m. Monday. </p><p>Ramey was expected to appear in court Thursday. </p>

entries.title: Person of interest arrested in West Side slayings of Uber driver, high school basketball player: source
entries.summary: <p>A person of interest is being questioned in the double homicide of a man who was driving for Uber and an 18-year-old basketball player who was his passenger, according to a law enforcement source. </p><p>The person, a 17-year-old boy, was arrested Wednesday afternoon, the source said. </p><p>Jassen Cho, 38, and Damarion Johnson, 18, were driving in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/08/high-school-senior-and-man-38-gunned-down-in-garfield-park-neighborhood" target="_blank" >200 block of North Homan Avenue</a> around 8:30 p.m. May 7 when someone inside a gray SUV fired at them.</p><p>A $10,000 reward was being offered by Cook County Crime Stoppers.</p><p><i>This is a developing story. Check back for updates.</i></p>

entries.title: Trump administration remains unreliable Second Amendment ally
entries.summary: <p>After the Supreme Court <a class="Link" href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/21pdf/20-843_7j80.pdf" target="_blank" >clarified</a> the constitutional test for gun control laws in 2022, many long-standing restrictions on the right to arms looked newly vulnerable. Second Amendment groups jumped at the opportunity, filing one lawsuit after another in cases that frequently pitted them against the Biden administration.</p><p>Those groups now have a powerful ally in the Trump administration, which has filed several lawsuits aimed at vindicating Americans' gun rights, including two filed last week in Colorado. But even as the Justice Department advertises its commitment to defending the Second Amendment, its position in other gun cases <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/04/09/trump-v-second-amendment/" target="_blank" >belies</a> that stance.</p><p>The Colorado lawsuits involve the state's <a class="Link" href="https://www.justice.gov/crt/media/1439591/dl?utm_medium=email&utm_source=govdelivery" target="_blank" >15-round magazine limit</a> and Denver's <a class="Link" href="https://www.justice.gov/crt/media/1439466/dl?utm_medium=email&utm_source=govdelivery" target="_blank" >“assault weapon” ban</a>. Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general in charge of the Justice Department's civil rights division, <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/05/07/doj-challenges-denvers-assault-weapon-ban-and-colorados-magazine-limit/" target="_blank" >argues</a> that both laws are unconstitutional for the same reason: They ban arms "in common use" for "lawful purposes," which the Supreme Court has <a class="Link" href="https://tile.loc.gov/storage-services/service/ll/usrep/usrep554/usrep554570/usrep554570.pdf" target="_blank" >said</a> are covered by the Second Amendment, and there is no "historical tradition" that would justify such a policy, as required by the test that the court prescribed in 2022.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-4d0000" name="module-4d0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>Last December, Dhillon <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/12/24/the-doj-assails-d-c-s-assault-weapon-ban-as-an-arbitrary-historically-ungrounded-gun-law/" target="_blank" >deployed</a> the same argument against the District of Columbia's "assault weapon" ban in <a class="Link" href="https://www.justice.gov/crt/media/1421731/dl" target="_blank" >another lawsuit</a> filed by the civil rights division's newly established <a class="Link" href="https://www.justice.gov/crt/second-amendment-section" target="_blank" >Second Amendment section</a>. Although federal appeals courts so far have not been receptive to such challenges, at least four Supreme Court justices — Clarence Thomas, Samuel Alito, Brett Kavanaugh, and Neil Gorsuch — seem inclined to agree with Dhillon.</p><p>That suggests the Supreme Court may soon weigh in on the constitutionality of "assault weapon" bans, which typically target rifles based on <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2018/05/14/assault-weapons-explained/" target="_blank" >arbitrarily disfavored features</a> such as pistol grips, folding stocks and flash suppressors. While the outcome of such a case is uncertain, Dhillon's argument seems like a straightforward application of principles the court has already recognized.</p><p>Dhillon is on even firmer ground in her Dec. 16 <a class="Link" href="https://www.justice.gov/crt/media/1420996/dl" target="_blank" >lawsuit</a> against the government of the U.S. Virgin Islands, which imposes a vague, highly discretionary requirement for publicly carrying handguns that is strikingly similar to the New York law that the Supreme Court overturned in 2022. Her <a class="Link" href="https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/us-department-justice-announces-second-amendment-pattern-or-practice-investigation" target="_blank" >investigation</a> of the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department, which takes as long as 18 months to act on carry permit applications, likewise seems consistent with the court's concerns about bureaucratic burdens on the right to bear arms.</p><p>The legal hook for the Justice Department's involvement in these cases is a <a class="Link" href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/34/12601" target="_blank" >federal law</a> that authorizes the attorney general to seek civil remedies for a law enforcement "pattern or practice of conduct" that deprives people of their constitutional or statutory rights. "The Constitution is not a suggestion," acting Attorney General Todd Blanche <a class="Link" href="https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-sues-city-denver-unconstitutional-weapons-bans" target="_blank" >said</a> last week, "and the Second Amendment is not a second-class right."</p><p>The Justice Department nevertheless <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/12/10/the-doj-says-it-will-challenge-unconstitutional-gun-policies-maybe-it-should-stop-defending-them/" target="_blank" >maintains</a> that the Second Amendment does not apply to broad categories of Americans who are barred from owning firearms based on criteria that have little or nothing to do with public safety. The Trump administration has defended the Gun Control Act's <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/10/20/scotus-will-consider-the-constitutionality-of-the-federal-ban-on-gun-possession-by-illegal-drug-users/" target="_blank" >ban</a> on firearm possession by "unlawful" drug users, which is at the center of a <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/03/02/scotus-seems-skeptical-of-the-federal-ban-on-gun-possession-by-cannabis-consumers/" target="_blank" >case</a> that the Supreme Court will soon decide, and that law's <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/06/12/17-years-ago-she-lost-her-gun-rights-for-passing-a-bad-check-she-wants-scotus-to-rectify-that-injustice/" target="_blank" >disarmament</a> of people with nonviolent felony records, which has generated many petitions that the justices so far have declined to accept.</p><p>Both of those controversies pit the Trump administration against the National Rifle Association and other leading gun rights groups. It is not hard to see why, since neither policy is supported by the sort of "historical tradition" that the Supreme Court has said is required to justify gun regulations.</p><p>The Justice Department insists that "the Second Amendment is not a second-class right." Yet it argues that cannabis consumers and people convicted of nonviolent felonies are, in effect, second-class citizens.</p><p>Unlike the civil liberties guaranteed by other constitutional amendments, the Trump administration says, the right to arms can be revoked for arbitrary reasons. Contrary to Blanche's rhetoric, that sure seems like a second-class right.</p><p><i>Jacob Sullum is a senior editor at Reason magazine.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-4c0000" name="module-4c0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>
entries.author: Jacob Sullum

entries.title: Dear Abby: Three's a crowd in family's housing arrangement
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> A few years ago, my husband and I bought a home together with his sister. We share the bills and chores and, for the most part, it works. We live in a nicer home than we could afford on our own.</p><p>Frequently, though, my husband and his sister have discussions and make decisions regarding the house without including me. I have complained loudly and clearly each time I've learned this has happened. I don't always find out. Usually, they'll apologize, but the behavior does not change.</p><p>We have recently experienced significant damage to the house from a bad storm. Insurance and contractors will be involved. I have already learned about decisions that were made without my input. I think this is highly disrespectful, and I'm ready to move out. I would love your advice. — <i>DISCOUNTED IN FLORIDA</i></p><p><b>DEAR DISCOUNTED:</b> You need to make your husband and your sister-in-law understand that you are an equal partner in this deal. Why they think your input is of little value is anyone's guess. Whether this will require the help of a mediator or marriage counselor depends upon how cooperative they are willing to be. However, if you continue to be ignored, you may want to consult a lawyer about what your legal rights are in this situation.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My husband and I lost our precious, beloved little dog a month ago. We have had other pets over the years, but as we got older, our little guy was like a child to us. He went everywhere with us.</p><p>We are having a terrible time handling this. For example, we went into the grocery store yesterday, and when we got to the pet food aisle, we both started crying. We cry every night at bedtime as we say goodnight to him in heaven. If we drive by a park where we walked him, we fall apart again. How can we cope? If we talk to friends or neighbors, we start crying again. Please help. — <i>PET PARENT IN MICHIGAN</i></p><p><b>DEAR PET PARENT:</b> Please accept my sympathy. The passing of a beloved furry family member is never easy. Because your loss is fresh, it's no wonder that you and your husband are grieving. Contact your veterinarian, explain your emotional state and ask for a referral to a grief support group. (Yes, they do exist.) With time, your overwhelming emotions will ease, and you will remember "the little guy" and be able to smile again.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> Because the cost of cards and postage is so high, I have started sending fancy e-cards for many occasions (except Christmas). I spend as much time selecting the right e-card as I would in a store selecting a paper card. I do send paper cards to friends and family who have expressed a preference. Are e-cards less acceptable than paper cards? — <i>SENDER OF GREETINGS IN OREGON</i></p><p><b>DEAR SENDER:</b> E-cards have gained in popularity for the reasons you mentioned. I do not consider them less appropriate (or welcome) than paper cards. It's the thought that counts. Readers, would you like to weigh in on this? I am interested in your opinion.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p><p>To order "How to Write Letters for All Occasions," send your name and mailing address, plus check or money order for $8 (U.S. funds) to: Dear Abby — Letter Booklet, P.O. Box 446, Kings Mills, OH 45034-0446. (Shipping and handling are included in the price.)</p>
entries.author: Abigail Van Buren

entries.title: Redistricting, while damaging, could send Black voters back to Democrats
entries.summary: <p>Over the past six months, Democrats have been more than happy to let President Donald Trump be their best campaign ad. From his ill-advised war in Iran to his ill-advised tariffs, his obvious declining mental acuity to his increasing desire to spend taxpayer money on wasteful vanity projects, Dems know that Politics 101 dictates you never interrupt your enemy when he’s making a mistake.</p><p>With politicos predicting a midterm election bloodbath for Republicans, Dems were riding high. That is, until Trump unleashed his redistricting wars.</p><p>Aware of their inability to win with the current maps, the GOP has been redrawing the country in its image, and potentially marginalizing minority voters in the process. That’s bad — for the left, but more importantly for democracy. Voters should choose their candidates, not the other way around.</p><p>But the right’s assault on Black voters in particular may not be the coup they seem to think it is, especially if it unintentionally helps the left shore up one of its most problematic gaps.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-1d0000" name="module-1d0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>In 2016, Trump won his first presidential election largely thanks to white voters, who made up 88% of his coalition. Then, only 1% of his voters were Black.</p><p>By 2024, just eight years later, Trump had expanded that coalition considerably, winning 15% of the Black vote, <a class="Link" href="https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2025/06/26/behind-trumps-2024-victory-a-more-racially-and-ethnically-diverse-voter-coalition/" target="_blank" >per Pew</a>.</p><p>But over on the Democrats’ side, the arrows were moving in the opposite direction. A once-reliable coalition — former President Barack Obama, for example, <a class="Link" href="https://ropercenter.cornell.edu/how-groups-voted-2008" target="_blank" >won</a> 95% of the Black vote in 2008 — has been incrementally leaving the Democratic Party or staying home. In 2024, Kamala Harris won just 83% of the Black vote, down from Joe Biden’s 87% in 2000.</p><p>I assume that’s worrisome to the Democratic Party, though we don’t know how worrisome because it has refused to release its 2024 autopsy.</p><p>What I do know is Trump and Republicans may have just given them a lifeline they weren’t expecting.</p><p>The redistricting forever wars have Republicans carving up predominantly Black majority districts nationwide. On nearly every metaphorical battlefield, the GOP is winning — Trump successfully primaried Indiana state lawmakers who refused to redistrict; the Supreme Court sliced into the Voting Rights Act; Virginia’s supreme court ruled against the Dems’ efforts to redistrict. According to CNN’s redistricting tracker, Republicans could net nine seats in November.</p><p>That’s unequivocally bad news for the left, but the unintended consequence of the right’s zeal to rig the maps could send Black voters back to the Dems in numbers a single candidate not named Obama could not.</p><p>“Democrats are gonna be able to go into African American communities and say, ‘Republicans are doing everything they can to take away your political power,’ ” Democratic strategist Ian Russell <a class="Link" href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/05/12/republicans-redistricting-democrats-black-hispanic-districts-midterm-message-00915565" target="_blank" >told Politico</a>. “That’s a really salient message.”</p><p>And it could come at a really important time. Turnout among Black voters in the last midterms <a class="Link" href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2023/05/02/black-voter-turnout-election-2022/" target="_blank" >dropped</a> by nearly 10 percentage points, from 51.7% in 2018 to 42% in 2022, whereas white turnout dropped just 1.5 points. The gap in 2022 was the largest in any election — presidential or midterm — since 2000.</p><p>Black voters’ disillusionment with Democrats has been growing, with just 66% self-affiliating with the party in 2023. The Republican war on Black districts could pull them back, at least in the short term.</p><p>Looking ahead, Democrats simply don’t have a transformative figure, like an Obama or a Bill Clinton, waiting in the wings to rebuild the Black coalition, but they do have an issue that could motivate it significantly.</p><p>If the Dems had a plan to win back this important voting bloc, or the parts of it that left, we don’t know what it was. But the redistricting wars might just be the catalyst they needed, and at the perfect time.</p><p><i>S.E. Cupp is the host of “S.E. Cupp Unfiltered” on CNN.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-6e0000" name="module-6e0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>
entries.author: S. E. Cupp

entries.title: Illinois politicians spend millions in campaign funds on meals, sometimes at swanky restaurants
entries.summary: <p>A swanky spot long anchoring Rush Street and the Gold Coast, Gibsons Bar & Steakhouse describes itself online as “a Chicago icon” that, besides its tasty Angus beef, offers “fresh fish, classic cocktails, an extensive wine list and exceptional service.”</p><p>“Celebrities, Chicago visitors and loyal neighborhood residents enjoy our three distinct locations: Chicago, Rosemont and Oak Brook.”</p><p>What could be added to Gibsons' marketing materials: They’re also a huge draw for politicians, with Illinois campaign funds spending more than $1.8 million at the establishments — including Gibsons Italia in the West Loop — on fundraising events, meetings and meals since the 1990s, according to a review of Illinois State Board of Elections disclosure records that also shows:<br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-c8621912-4d84-11f1-8e8b-63b7b5b6ec16"><li>Roughly $900,000 was spent by campaign funds over the last two decades at Harry Caray’s restaurants, with the main locale just north of the Chicago River at 33 W. Kinzie St.<br></li><li>More than $800,000 was spent at the Rosebud restaurants, with its signature spot long situated in Little Italy.<br></li><li>Erie Cafe, at 536 W. Erie St., has been paid more than $450,000 by campaign funds dating to the late 1990s — with former Cook County Assessor Joseph Berrios’ political accounts responsible for roughly a third of that tally.<br></li><li>Petterino’s, in the Downtown theater district, was paid more than $400,000, while RPM restaurants in the Loop were paid a similar amount.<br></li><li>Chicago Cut Steakhouse, 300 N. that campaign cash is often raised only by virtue of a politician’s government position — and the more powerful the political figure, the more campaign money is often thrown their way by special interests craving influence.</p><p>If politicians are essentially living off their campaign funds and not paying income taxes on that, they could also face the wrath of the IRS.</p><p>Either way, it’s difficult to police whether a meal or a drink — or virtually any campaign spending in Illinois — is appropriate. </p><p>When reporting campaign spending to election regulators, political funds are Vazquez / Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>That includes $531 spent at the Rush Street locale in January, with “meals” the only description of the expense. Neither Welch nor his aides could be reached.</p><p>Welch’s campaign fund also has been a recent spender at Chicago Cut, known for its meats, wines and ambience.</p><p>Until last August, there were apparently no payments from Welch’s campaign to Chicago Cut. But since then, the campaign paid for 11 meals at Chicago Cut totaling nearly $2,000.</p><p>Three of Welch’s visits were in 2026 and eight in 2025, with the bills ranging from more than $50 to $300 — which, by Chicago Cut’s prices, isn’t bad, no matter how you cut it.</p><p>After all, there’s a $99 bone-in 16-ounce filet on the menu, along with a $79 dijon herb-crusted rack of lamb.</p><p>All told, the Welch fund has spent more than $100,000 on what’s categorized as meals over the last four years.</p><p>Campaign funds for state Senate President Don Harmon (D-Oak Park) spent more than $230,000 on meals over the last two decades, from Panera and Domino’s Pizza to Vele, a Springfield restaurant that has received nearly $18,000 from Friends of Don Harmon for State Senate since 2022.</p><p>A Harmon campaign spokesman explains, “The Senate president frequently hosts member dinners with a half a dozen folks at a time to discuss legislation, concerns in their districts and family life.”</p><p>Meantime, the campaign funds for members of Congress from Illinois also at times made expenditures at restaurants back home, or in Washington, D.C., for fundraisers, meals and the like.</p><p>Overall, more than $40,000 was collectively spent at Chicago Cut, while about $25,000 was spent at the Capital Grille in Washington, according to Federal Election Commission records.</p>

entries.title: Convicted former Ald. Edward Burke's campaign money isn't radioactive to everyone
entries.summary: <p>Since his conviction on corruption charges and a brief prison stint that followed, politicians have surely kept their distance, at least publicly, from former Chicago Ald. Edward M. Burke.</p><p>Not so in two notable instances:<br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-7773e511-4d5c-11f1-a696-91d880f684e0"><li>Burke’s former City Council colleague, Ald. Ray Lopez (15th), recently accepted $10,000 in campaign contributions from two of Burke’s political accounts.<br></li><li>A campaign fund for George Alpogianis, mayor of north suburban Niles, recently accepted a $1,000 contribution from a Burke fund.</li></ul><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/usa-vs-edward-burke" >Convicted in 2023 </a>on extortion-related charges, Burke was released from prison last July and remained under the jurisdiction of the federal prison system into November, records show.</p><p>Throughout the ordeal, his campaign funds stayed open — and were used to cover hefty legal bills that appear to relate to his prosecution.</p><p>But otherwise the funds had been relatively dormant in terms of giving, and taking, donations.</p><p>Recent disclosure reports filed with the Illinois State Board of Elections, which regulates campaigns, show that the Burnham Committee, one of Burke’s campaign funds, gave Friends of Raymond A. Lopez $5,000 in a contribution dated Dec. 31.</p><p>Another $5,000 was given to the 15th Ward Regular Democratic Organization, which Lopez also oversees, by Friends of Edward M. Burke the same day.</p><p>A longtime political ally of Burke, Lopez stirred up controversy in 2023 as Burke was retiring — prior to his conviction and after more than 50 years in office — by proposing that May 15 of that year be called<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2023/4/17/23687282/ed-burke-day-resolution-chicago-city-council-ray-lopez-may-15-brandon-johnson-inauguration-mayor" > “Ald. Edward M. Burke Day” </a>in Chicago.</p><p>Lopez eventually dropped the effort at Burke’s request, as the Chicago Sun-Times reported at the time.</p><p>Burke, the former 14th Ward alderman, couldn’t be reached for comment.</p><p>His Burnham fund has more than $2 million on hand, records show.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-b60000" name="image-b60000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/cc96a67/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4937x2771+0+260/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe1%2F61%2F1af7ed9b451385b5c641f5461fc4%2Flopez-040722-13.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3dacbdd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4937x2771+0+260/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe1%2F61%2F1af7ed9b451385b5c641f5461fc4%2Flopez-040722-13.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b63fad4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4937x2771+0+260/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe1%2F61%2F1af7ed9b451385b5c641f5461fc4%2Flopez-040722-13.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Chicago Ald. Ray Lopez (15th)." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b63fad4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4937x2771+0+260/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe1%2F61%2F1af7ed9b451385b5c641f5461fc4%2Flopez-040722-13.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/90ff0a2/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4937x2771+0+260/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe1%2F61%2F1af7ed9b451385b5c641f5461fc4%2Flopez-040722-13.JPG 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b63fad4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4937x2771+0+260/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe1%2F61%2F1af7ed9b451385b5c641f5461fc4%2Flopez-040722-13.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Chicago 15th Ward Ald. Ray Lopez </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin / Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Lopez said of the campaign contributions: “I have long believed that returning citizens, after completing their court sentencing, should be welcomed back as productive citizens should they seek to move beyond their transgressions. I do not believe anyone’s mistakes are life sentences that extend beyond their punishment.”</p><p>Friends of Edward M. Burke — which has about $80,000 in cash on hand and more than $8 million invested — also gave $1,000 to Friends of George D. Alpogianis, records show.</p><p>Alpogianis has been mayor of Niles since 2021 and was reelected in April 2025 while running unopposed. Before that, he was a village trustee and served as chairman of Niles’ Finance Committee, the same post Burke held in Chicago’s City Council for decades.</p><p>The campaign money, given by Burke’s fund in October, was made public in disclosure reports this year.</p><p>Alpogianis is part of a Chicago restaurant group that includes a number of establishments in the Chicago region and out-of-state, from a hot dog chain and a healthy food shop at O’Hare Airport to Kappy’s Restaurant & Pancake House in north suburban Morton Grove.</p><p>Alpogianis said he grew up in the North Side’s 40th Ward volunteering under then-Ald. Patrick O’Connor, and his family once owned the Palace Grill on the Near West Side. Through all of that, Alpogianis said he came to know a lot of people, including Burke, who would become one of his political mentors.</p><p>“I’m not one to judge anybody,” Alpogianis said, referring to Burke’s felony case. “Good people sometimes make bad decisions. I just know him in a very different capacity. I have a great deal of respect for him.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-300000" He heard about it; he sent me a check.”</p><p>Burke’s conviction involved his attempts to muscle certain businesses into hiring his longtime law firm, Klafter & Burke, for property tax appeals work.</p><p>The Kappy’s property is owned by another company that’s used the now-defunct firm.</p><p>Likewise, Klafter & Burke and another lawyer who used to work there and is now a partner with Burke's daughter, Jennifer Burke, have handled tax-related appeals for Alpogianis’ home over the years, county records show.</p><p>Alpogianis said he’s the one who wanted to bring them on — “they never approached me about doing it” — and Edward M. Burke has never spoken to him about any of this.</p><p>Burke’s campaign funds have also continued giving contributions to Catholic organizations, even though the arm of the church for Cook and Lake counties led by Cardinal Blase Cupich, the Archdiocese of Chicago, once contemplated whether it should be taking Burke’s money given his criminal case.</p><p>In March, the Burnham fund gave the archdiocese $10,000, records show.</p><p>In June, the Burnham fund gave $1,000 to the Augustinian religious order that Pope Leo XIV belongs to.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/02/14/edward-burke-joy-cunningham-campaign-contributions-illinois-supreme-court-burnham-committee" target="_blank" >Illinois Supreme Court justice’s campaign took $40K contribution from crooked ex-Chicago alderman</a> </li> </ul> </div> <div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2024/06/27/alderman-edward-burke-chicago-judge-virginia-kendall-corruption-catholic-church-campaign-donations-cardinal-cupich" target="_blank" >Ex-Ald. as part of Hubbard Street’s May 14, 15 and 17 performances at the Harris Theater for Music and Dance.</p><p>This season-ending appearance back in the contemporary company’s hometown comes just weeks after a high-profile two-week run at the Joyce Theater in New York, one of this country’s most important dance venues.</p><p>For her fourth and final commission, Hubbard Street leaders gave Barton free rein – no strictures or parameters of any kind. “That’s the beauty here. Make what you want to make,” said the choreographer, who has worked with everyone from Mikhail Baryshnikov and Cyndi Lauper to the English National Ballet.</p><div class="Enhancement" The result is non-narrative and titled “LubDub,” drawing on a medical term that describes the familiar pattern of the human heartbeat.</p><p>Asked to discuss the movement vocabulary she employs here, Barton demurred. But when the descriptor “unruly” was suggested, she was quick to embrace it.</p><p>“That’s a good word for it,” she said. “I really feel I’m at that place right now where I want to scream it out loud and share. I’m so pissed off at the way the world is right now, and I see how dancers work together, and I’m so inspired by their willingness to work as a collective. And I’m wanting to share that energy.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-320000" name="module-320000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3><b>Hubbard Street Dance Chicago</b></h3><b>When</b>: 7:30 p.m. May 14 and 15 and 2 p.m. May 17<br><b>Where</b>: Harris Theater for Music and Dance, 205 E. Spasmodic jerks of the body. A male dancer shuffling haltingly along in a kind of squat position, with another seated dancer wrapped over one of his legs.</p><p>The work’s predominantly electronic score combines the music of three composers – Jlin, a Chicago-based musician who has worked with everyone from Bjork to multimedia artist Nick Cave; Kara-Lis Coverdale of Montreal, Quebec, and Norwegian folk fiddler Susanne That project established an ongoing bond with the company that has climaxed with her current three-year residency.</p><p>When Linda-Denise Fisher-Harrell took over as Hubbard Street’s artistic director in March 2021, she quickly asked Barton to return to stage “Busk.” The new company leader had long admired Barton’s dreamlike 2009 work, which is set to Gypsy and choral music with the dancers in layered black costumes, including hoods at one point, and thought it would be ideal for Hubbard Street.</p><p>That collaboration went so well that Barton approached Fisher-Harrell about the possibility of a residency. entries.title: Two men gunned down in separate West, Southwest Side attacks
entries.summary: <p>Two men were killed in separate shootings two hours apart Thursday morning on the city's Southwest Side and West Sides.</p><p>Most recently, a 54-year-old man was found shot about 8:20 a.m. outside in the 3900 block of West 86th Street in Ashburn suffering from gunshot wounds to the body, police said. He was taken to Mount Sinai Hosp9ital, where he was pronounced dead. </p><p>Earlier, at 6:15 a.m. in the 3900 block of West Flournoy Street in Garfield Park, a 19-year-old man was getting into his car when several assailants armed with guns exited a blue car and confronted the 19-year-old and shot him, police said. </p><p>The gunmen fled and the 19-year-old was pronounce dead at the scene, after suffering multiple gunshot wounds to the body, police said. </p><p>No one was arrested and area detectives are investigating both homicides. <br></p>

entries.title: 2 shot, critically injured in Edgewater
entries.summary: <p>Two people were shot and critically injured in Edgewater Thursday morning, according to Chicago Fire Department officials. </p><p>The shooting happened sometime before 7:30 a.m. in the 6200 block of North Glenwood Avenue, authorities said. </p><p>Two people were taken to an area hospital where they were in critical condition, fire officials said. </p><p>Chicago police were responding to a call of service in the area but have not yet released additional details. </p><p>A 30-year resident of the neighborhood says she heard someone screamed "what the f - - -" multiple times before at least three or four gunshots rang out.</p><p>Some residents in the area were shaken up or stunned by the shooting, while others were more mildly surprised. </p><p>"This is the first time someone's been shot in such close proximity to where I live," said Nancy Onderdonk, another resident of 30 years. "When [gun violence] comes this close, that's when people hopefully get more involved."</p><p><i>This is a developing story. Check back for updates.</i></p>

entries.title: City/Suburban Hoops Report: Grant Mordini heads to Kansas, locals eye USA hoops, E. Peoria star transfers
entries.summary: <p>The Class of 2027 in Illinois came into high school with plenty of hype several years ago. They immediately shined, including unprecedented freshmen seasons from the likes of Davion Thompson at Bolingbrook and Jaxson Davis at Warren.</p><p>But there were other high-profile players. Kenwood’s Devin Cleveland was touted as perhaps the best of the bunch, while Quinton Kitt at East Peoria quickly emerged as a high-major prospect.</p><p>Those four, along with Illinois commit Mason Martin of Neuqua Valley, will all play high-major college basketball. But with this week’s announcement that Kitt, another Illinois commitment, is leaving East Peoria, three of the five will finish their high school careers at prep schools.</p><p>Thompson and Cleveland left following their sophomore years for Link Academy and La Lumiere, respectively, while Kitt will finish up his final year at a still-to-be-determined prep school.</p><p>This is a huge blow for an East Peoria team that would undoubtedly have been one of the state’s elite teams after winning a school-record 29 games last season. With Kitt, along with super-charged scoring lead guard Cole DuBois, a pair of players who have already surpassed 1,000-points in their career, this set up to be the best team in school history.</p><p>With what he had coming back and what was at stake in this 2026-27 season, coach Jarrett Brown went out to upgrade the Raiders schedule. East Peoria was set to play in several high-profile events, including a date at next year’s When Sides Collide event at Benet.</p><p><b>Jaxson Davis, Brady Pettigrew and USA Basketball</b></p><p>Historically, the USA Basketball experience has been a springboard for a high school player’s development.</p><p>That’s an added plus for two of the state’s top talents: Warren’s Jaxson Davis and Bolingbrook’s Brady Pettigrew. Both have their eyes on playing with USA Basketball this summer for their respective age group teams.</p><p>It’s no surprise the state’s best player, Davis, is on the cusp of potentially adding another accomplishment to his growing resume.</p><p>Davis participated in USA Basketball’s April minicamp in Indianapolis. Now he’s headed to the U18 trials at the Olympic training center in Colorado Springs later this month.</p><p>The Sun-Times Player of the Year, who plays with Meanstreets on Nike’s EYBL circuit in the spring and summer, has been courted heavily by the likes of Michigan, Iowa, Northwestern and Marquette.</p><p>Pettigrew, a consensus top 25 player nationally in the Class of 2028, plays with Bradley Beal Elite on the EYBL circuit. The 6-4 guard will head to the U17 Team USA World Cup team tryouts in the middle of June.</p><p><b>Lake Forest’s Grant Mordini headed to Kansas</b></p><p>Grant Mordini was always an intriguing but late-developing prospect while playing for coach Phil LaScala at Lake Forest.</p><p>The 6-11 Mordini, a 2025 Lake Forest graduate, headed to prep school for a year following high school. He played this past season at Avon Old Farms School in Connecticut, garnering some Division I interest, including an offer from Missouri-Kansas City.</p><p>But in this day of roster building and scholarship numbers growing to 15 at the Division I level, the size, skill and potential of Mordini will bring added attention. It all caught the eye of Kansas.</p><p>Mordini, who averaged 12.5 points and 8.5 rebounds a game at Avon Old Farms, committed and signed with the Jayhawks last week.<br></p>

href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wdkodt-l-k/" target="_blank" >Sophie Sherry</a>, <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wdkodt-l-u/" target="_blank" >Jon Seidel</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wdkodt-l-o/" target="_blank" >Esther Yoon-Ji Kang</a></h5><p><b>Ready to sue</b>: Eighteen people caught up in last fall’s notorious military-style raid on a South Shore apartment complex took a key step this week toward holding the federal government legally accountable for "brutalizing and racially profiling" the building’s residents, attorneys say. </p><p><b>What they want</b>: The MacArthur Justice Center and other legal groups said they’d submitted administrative complaints against the U.S. Department of Homeland Security in pursuit of relief under the Federal Tort Claims Act, which offers a path to suing federal agencies. The 18 are seeking $5 million each, in addition to property damages. If the feds deny the claim or fail to respond within six months, attorneys can move forward with a lawsuit.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: The Sept. 30 raid became an early flashpoint of Operation Midway Blitz. Agents descended on the complex from helicopters, used flashbang grenades to burst through doors and pointed guns at residents, according to the new filing. Residents reported seeing men, women and children dragged out of their apartments and zip-tied. Here's what to know: </p><p><b>Why the Bears want to move</b>: To make more money. Soldier Field is the smallest stadium in the NFL, and the Bears rent it from the Chicago Park District. </p><p><b>Where could they go?</b>: Arlington Heights or Hammond, Indiana, are the only choices at this point, according to the team. But they’ve waffled on their preferred destination over the past few years.</p><p><b>Are they definitely leaving?</b>: Yes, barring a sudden change of heart. Mayor Brandon Johnson cheered alongside Bears president Kevin Warren for their lakefront proposal in 2024, but Gov. JB Pritzker and legislative leaders threw cold water on that expensive pitch.</p><p><b>The stakes</b>: No Chicago legislator wants to be held responsible for letting the team leave the city. barbecue to Chicago’s masses</a></h3><p></p><h5>By <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wdkodt-l-tl/" target="_blank" >Amy Yee</a></h5><p>KFire owners Ben Kim and Eddie Hwang launched their first location in Logan Square in July 2020, at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic. Many restaurants struggled when government lockdowns crashed business, and grappled with challenges including soaring inflation and supply chain delays.</p><p>KFire weathered the turbulence, and in 2023 opened its Old Town location, where much of its catering business is now based. That business is growing at double-digit rates and accounts for one-third of sales.</p><p>"We were surprised at how big it got," said Kim, who previously worked as a financial analyst in New York.</p><p>Customers want Korean barbecue, especially KFire’s signature dish: Kalbi, or beef short ribs. Korean food and kalbi have special significance for Hwang, who grew up in Morton Grove, and Kim, who’s from New Jersey.</p><p>"Some of my fondest memories as a child are family gatherings for special occasions," Kim said. "Those were the times we’d bring out the kalbi. It was a special meal we shared when everyone was together, like at a family picnic or camping trip."</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wdkodt-l-tr/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p>Yesterday, we asked you: <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wdkodt-l-tj/" target="_blank" >Do you think e-bikes should be allowed on the Lake Shore trail?</a></p><p>Here’s some of what you said, edited for length and clarity…</p><p>"E-bikes, yes, with lower speeds. Electric motorcycles, no. Fat tire motor bikes, no — they are just too fast and dangerous." — <i>Tom Krajecki</i></p><p>"Yes, as long as they follow a speed limit of no more than 10-15 mph!" — <i>D. Buerkett</i></p><p>"As an avid bike path user on e-bikes and pedal bikes, I’ve not seen any problems with the integration of e-bikes ... In fact, I find that the bike paths along the lake have become more accessible ... to those with physical challenges that preclude them from using a pedal bike." — <i>Nicole Cantello</i></p><p>"I think e-bikes should be allowed on the lakefront trail ... Many people still do not feel safe riding their bikes on the street, so prohibiting e-bikes on the trail would reduce the number of people biking in this city. Better solutions would be widening the trail to allow for more cyclists or adding more protected bike lanes in the city to give people other routes." — <i>Andrea Bryson</i></p><p>"The problem with e-bikes is the same as the problem with cars. Most people ride responsibly, go at appropriate speeds, pay attention to those around them. On a nice weekend day in the summer when traffic quadruples, so do the number of idiots ... Sadly e-bikes should be banned, at least on weekends." — <i>Jonathan Speigel</i></p><hr><p>Thanks for reading the Sun-Times Morning Edition!<br>Got a story you think we missed? <a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >Email us here.</a></p><hr><p><b>Written and curated by</b>: Matt Moore<br><b>Editor</b>: Eydie Cubarrubia<br><b>Hat tip</b>: Sun-Times' Joel Carlson for today's subject line, which you'll find on <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wdkodt-l-tt/" target="_blank" >the front page of today’s newspaper</a> — on newsstands and online now.</p><hr><p> <br><i>The Chicago Sun-Times is a nonprofit supported by readers like you. entries.title: Knife-wielding man commandeers CTA bus with passengers 6 miles off route, ending with Near North Side arrest
entries.summary: <p>A 57-year-old woman driving a CTA bus made a daring escape from a window early Wednesday when a knife-wielding man commandeered her bus, making her drive off its route for several miles, sources say. </p><p>According to a law enforcement source, passengers were also aboard the bus during the kidnapping. </p><p>No one was injured, and charges were pending against the man, who was arrested on the city's Near North Side after a CTA supervisor tracked the bus, police said. </p><p>The attack unfolded about 2:40 a.m. aboard the No. 53 Pulaski bus in the 2400 block of North Pulaski Road, police and the CTA said. </p><p>A man riding the bus suddenly pulled a sharp object and demanded the bus "not stop," making her drive off her route by nearly six miles away, into the city's Near North Side, police said.</p><p>The driver complied, but not long after was able to climb out a window, police said. </p><p>A CTA supervisor was able to track the bus and the suspect fled but was quickly arrested in the 100 block of West Chestnut Street. </p><p>In a statement, the CTA — which is pushing for felony charges — praised police for their "swift actions" leading to the "immediate apprehension" of the suspect. The agency did respond to inquiries about passengers but did say it will work closely with law enforcement to assist the investigation.</p>

entries.title: Chicago native Joe Musso hosting new post-round golf show at CBS Sports
entries.summary: <p>CBS Sports’ Joe Musso caught David Kaplan’s eye long before Musso caught the eye of CBS.</p><p>Musso, a Chicago native who grew up in the Galewood neighborhood, played wide receiver at Illinois Wesleyan on the same football team as Kaplan’s stepson Garret Laflamme.</p><p>“He reminded me of [former Bears receiver] Tom Waddle,” said Kaplan, then a host at Comcast SportsNet Chicago. “He was not the fastest but the toughest. This guy would take a hit. I said, I wanna meet that dude.”</p><p>Musso wanted to meet Kaplan, too, but for a different reason. He wanted to be a broadcaster.</p><p>“I went up to him at a tailgate and said, I’m really interested in getting into the business,” Musso said. “He goes, You’re my intern this summer.”</p><p>In 2011, Musso interned at CSN, jumpstarting a career that now has him at CBS Sports, where he’s hosting “Scorecard,” a PGA post-round show that debuted this year and will air after each round of the PGA Championship this week on CBS Sports HQ, the Golf on CBS YouTube channel and Paramount+.</p><p>After graduating, Musso worked at CSN as a production assistant, connecting with talents such as Pat Boyle, Chuck Garfien and Sarah Kustok. But he was itching to work on the other side of the camera.</p><p>“I’m enjoying being a part of this, but I think I want to do that version of it,” Musso said of his thinking at the time. “How much fun it looked like they were having. We’re talking about Blackhawks Cup runs, the Cubs trending toward being something.”</p><p>After attending Northwestern’s Medill School of Journalism, Musso worked at CBS affiliates in Lincoln, Nebraska, and Sacramento, California, before joining the nascent CBS Sports HQ in 2019. A passionate golfer, he worked to put his stamp on the channel’s golf coverage.</p><p>That led to “Scorecard,” which is a casual, comfortable and informative watch.</p><p>“I feel like myself and Shane Bacon, who even before being co-host, have been golf buddies,” Musso said. “So I think that like the conversation started well before the show started, which has allowed us to hit the ground running.</p><p>“One of our executives said, The show made me wanna crack a beer and watch it with you guys. That’s exactly what we’re going for.”</p><p>Kaplan was impressed with Musso’s work as an intern 15 years ago. He’s even more so now.</p><p>“Joe has ‘it,’ ” Kaplan said. “If I were a news director in Chicago looking for a sportscaster, that’d be the first call I’d make.”<br></p>
